title: Who’ll pay for overruns on the Darlington small modular reactor? Plus other unanswered questions
html:
The Darlington Nuclear Generating Station in Clarington, Ont. The new project contemplates building four small modular reactors known as BWRX-300s, a model that has never been built before.Sammy Kogan/The Globe and Mail

Just months into construction, Canada’s most ambitious nuclear project in four decades has already suffered serious setbacks.

Construction of a new nuclear power plant officially began in April when the foundation for its first reactor building was set in place. Located in Clarington, Ont., Ontario Power Generation’s Darlington New Nuclear Project (DNNP) contemplates building four small modular reactors (SMRs) known as BWRX-300s, a model that has never been built before. The project’s overall budget was $20.9-billion, $7.7-billion of which was for the first unit. But on Nov. 10, OPG announced that it no longer expects that first reactor to meet its approved budget, nor will it enter service by October 2030 as promised.

Nuclear projects are notorious for suffering massive cost overruns and taking far longer than promised, often with significant consequences for consumers. Here’s what to know about the DNNP’s setbacks, and what past failed nuclear projects reveal about what might happen next.

How bad are the overruns?

OPG is offering few details, however the original budget already included significant contingencies and escalations intended to cushion setbacks. The utility said it launched “a comprehensive assessment” to determine a new schedule and budget, expected to be completed by mid-2027.

OPG did not respond to queries from The Globe and Mail about which aspects of the project are behind schedule. An analysis of OPG disclosures by The Globe suggests key project milestones have already been missed by months.

For example, OPG was to have completed assembly of a tunnel-boring machine by February 2026. But that was achieved sometime during the three months ended Sept. 30.

OPG’s deadline for drilling the station’s marine intake was Oct. 31. However, as of Nov. 10, OPG reports show it had not yet even commenced tunnel boring; it expected to do so by the end of this year.

How much those and other delays set back the project as a whole isn’t apparent, but there are hints. The timing of OPG’s original plan – reflected in its Dec. 2025 rate application to the Ontario Energy Board, covering 2027 through 2031 – indicated the first unit would begin generating electricity in October 2030. In a Nov. 10 report, the OPG notified the Ontario Energy Board that it would remove the DNNP entirely from the application, suggesting startup will be not before 2031, making it at least 14 months late. However, that is not definitive: The same document elsewhere contemplated the possibility Unit 1 might enter service earlier.

What caused the overruns?

OPG is offering few details, however the original budget already included significant contingencies and escalations intended to cushion setbacks.Sammy Kogan/The Globe and Mail

In financial statements published Nov. 10, OPG attributed the overruns to GE Vernova Hitachi Nuclear Energy’s “ongoing engineering” work. That, in turn, “has impacts on construction execution and supply chain performance.”

GE Vernova Hitachi is responsible for designing the BWRX-300 reactor at the plant’s heart, as well as procuring major components and providing engineering and support. OPG began construction without a detailed set of plans.

Why does that matter? Can’t OPG work on other parts of the project while GE Vernova Hitachi’s engineers catch up?

Such reasoning has spelled disaster for countless nuclear projects, particularly those involving “first-of-a-kind” reactors such as the BWRX-300. Much project management literature counsels proponents to not rush to begin construction, because problem-solving and delays cost a lot less during the planning phase.

Consider this: OPG’s financial statements indicate it’s spending roughly $100-million a month on the DNNP. Earlier this year, it reported having as many as 1,500 workers on site on a typical day.

“You don’t want to have 1,500 people just sitting around,” said Koroush Shirvan, an associate professor of nuclear engineering at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology.

“Because that’s going to eat through your budget and contingency very, very fast.”

Surely OPG was aware of these risks.

It was. In past interviews with The Globe, OPG officials said that the facility’s design would be sufficiently advanced that “first-of-a-kind” risks would be eliminated before construction began. In May 2025, Ontario’s government reported that “OPG has completed their engineering and design work for the first SMR” and developed a “‘high-confidence’ budget and schedule.”

When The Globe asked in May about the status of the BWRX-300’s detailed design, OPG replied that “standard plant design was substantially completed in December 2025 as planned.”

However, experts told The Globe that “standard plant design” is very different from “detailed” design. The latter includes three-dimensional representations of every pipe, cable and duct, exact weld specifications and a whole lot more. That’s what’s required to actually build a nuclear power plant. It’s unclear what detailed design work has been completed and what remains outstanding.

What happened to other nuclear plants that began construction without detailed plans?

Bad things.

France’s Flamanville-3, completed a dozen years behind schedule and massively over budget, offers a good example. A report by Jean-Martin Folz, former head of French automaker Peugeot, found that the plant’s construction began without a complete set of validated plans. The result was that the design continuously changed during construction, and lots of work had to be redone. Flamanville-3 blew its budget many times over.

In Burke County, Georgia, two units at the Alvin W. Vogtle plant, the U.S.’s largest nuclear station, began construction in 2009; they were the first to feature Westinghouse’s AP1000 reactor. The U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission licensed the AP1000’s design prior to completion, but the missing elements led to myriad problems during construction and huge cost overruns. Similar problems occurred with two nearly identical AP1000s in South Carolina, V.C. Summer Units 2 and 3, which were abandoned in 2017 after billions of dollars had been spent.

“These lessons have been repeated over and over and over again,” Dr. Shirvan said.

The financial fallout from Vogtle and V.C. Summer led to the bankruptcy of Westinghouse, the main contractor and reactor designer on both projects.

Who’ll pay for the DNNP overruns?

The Toronto skyline is seen behind the Darlington Nuclear Generating Station in Clarington, Ont.Sammy Kogan/The Globe and Mail

The DNNP is being executed under what’s referred to as a “integrated product delivery model,” under which OPG, GE Vernova Hitachi, architect-engineer AtkinsRéalis Group Inc. ATRL-T and construction company Aecon Group Inc. ARE-T share risks. A portion of their fees can be withheld if certain objectives aren’t met. A senior OPG executive told reporters in 2025 that if the DNNP went late or over budget, “all of us – the partners and OPG – will have to share the risk of that overrun.”

However, in a statement to The Globe, AtkinsRéalis spokesperson Daniela Pizzuto wrote that the overruns would not have a material financial impact on her company because “our risk is capped.”

Vogtle and V.C. Summer demonstrate how, even when private companies were contractually obligated to deliver a nuclear power plant under a fixed-price contract, the public ended up paying dearly. Georgia Power raised residential electricity rates significantly to cover Vogtle’s construction costs and overruns. South Carolina’s utility, Santee Cooper, owed US$3.6-billion for the unfinished V.C. Summer units, which its customers pay for on their monthly bills despite never receiving a single kilowatt hour.

“Contracts don’t fix problems, they fix blame,” said James Little, a member of South Carolina’s Governor’s Nuclear Advisory Council, in April at a hearing at which the potential restart of construction at V.C. Summer was discussed.

“Relying on contracts to manage risk, it’s a false hope.”

Who will protect Ontarians’ interests concerning the DNNP overruns?

The Ontario Energy Board sets the rates OPG can charge for electricity generated by its nuclear power plants, and is mandated to provide information to consumers. “We will never lose sight of the individual rate payers, the consumers, the people of Ontario,” the regulator asserts on its web site.

The Globe requested an interview with the OEB to explore how consumers might be exposed to the DNNP overruns. Spokesperson Tom Miller denied the request and said such questions should be directed to OPG.

Could overruns halt or kill the DNNP?

With the extent of the overruns unclear, it’s difficult to gauge OPG’s ability to adapt and respond. The utility reported that construction will continue. It did not answer questions about how it has adjusted its on-site work plans in response to incomplete engineering work. Aecon, the constructor, declined an interview request, as did GE Vernova Hitachi.

Critics of Ontario’s nuclear-focused electricity strategy were quick to pounce on the DNNP’s troubles; the Ontario Clean Air Alliance demanded its cancellation.

“The most head shaking part of this risky project is that Ontario willingly chose to be a guinea pig for an unproven American (GE-Hitachi) nuclear technology,” director Angela Bischoff wrote in a statement.

“While other jurisdictions stood back and said ‘after you,’ Ontario rushed forward and recklessly committed to a design that has not been built anywhere in the world.”

The provincial and federal governments have shown no indications they are reconsidering their commitments – and some observers say they shouldn’t.

Chris Gadomski, a nuclear analyst at BloombergNEF, said first-of-a-kind nuclear projects are exceptionally difficult to deliver, invariably suffer delays and are painfully expensive. It was “disheartening,” he added, that DNNP proponents hadn’t learned from Vogtle and V.C. Summer.

But, following missteps during construction of the first unit, “the question to be asking is: Will OPG and General Electric Hitachi learn from their mistakes and get the second, third and fourth one right?” he said.

“It would be a shame if they stopped after one…the worst thing they could possibly do is stop the project.”
summary: Nuclear projects are notorious for suffering cost overruns and taking longer than promised, often with consequences for consumers
